question: to the Commission Daniel Buda (PPE), Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

The abolition of the 2-pillar structure of the CAP has erased the complementarity and synergies between Pillar 2 and the rural development fund facet of cohesion policy. The EAFRD and the ERDF had separate objectives, and their merger into a single mega-fund in the future programming period will lead to competition for the same resources under the national and regional partnership plans, both between the two funds and between them and other programmes. Without substantial investment in rural areas, these will remain insufficiently attractive to tempt young people or convince them to stay and hence foster generational renewal, placing a question mark over long-term food security. The EUR 47.8 billion proposed as a minimum rural target by the Commission is insufficient if Member States’ ambition remains limited. Moreover, there is a total overlap between the rural target and the target of EUR 218 billion for less-developed regions. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that rural areas receive sufficient funding to guarantee their development and generational renewal, hence reversing demographic decline and eliminating talent development traps?
Has the Commission conducted a study into the impact on rural areas of the dismantling of the EAFRD and the ERDF?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2026) The proposal putting forward a single National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP)1 for each Member State (and an additional Interreg Plan) aims to address the current fragmented implementation of resources with a single rulebook approach, thus enhancing synergies between policies, increasing flexibility in resource allocation and use, as well as simplifying access to funding for beneficiaries. The impact assessment2 accompanying the Commission proposal for the NRPPs identified that combining the common agricultural policy, cohesion policy and other EU Funds in a single plan allowed Member States to provide the most effective and comprehensive support to rural areas, provided that appropriate strategies for rural areas are in place. Fostering attractiveness of territories and improving living standards in rural areas feature explicitly in the objectives of the future NRPPs. A rural spending target of 10% of each Member State’s envelope outside ringfenced amounts for the Common Agricultural Policy and the Common Fisheries Policy has been proposed to ensure continuity of investments in the development of rural territories. Member States and regions are expected to build a consistent agenda of measures on the basis of the reference framework set out in Article 22 of the proposal addressing rural areas’ specific needs and challenges and concentrate resources to foster diverse and resilient rural economies and support generational renewal, contributing to the right to stay. The rural spending target should be seen as a tool to ensure a comprehensive approach to address the needs and opportunities of rural areas, including outside less developed regions.
